newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Music fest guru Wein revels in Newport nostalgia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Music fest guru Wein revels in Newport nostalgia.

text.p: Who ever heard of a pop music impresario who turned down offers by Jimi Hendrix and the Rolling Stones to perform at his festival?

Meet George Wein. The 71-year-old jazz pianist and promoter founded the venerable Newport Jazz Festival -- the granddaddy of all modern outdoor pop festivals -- in 1954 and the equally legendary Newport Folk Festival -- scene of Bob Dylan's 1965 conversion to electrified music -- in 1959.

Four decades later, Wein's annual galas in blueblood Newport, Rhode Island, manage to retain a distinctive identity despite increasing competition from a horde of new festivals and travelling shows like Lollapalooza and Lilith Fair.
"Boy, is there competition," Wein told Reuters in an interview. "It's really tougher and tougher to keep the uniqueness of the festival."

This year's Newport programme unfolds in three separate events: the Rockport Rhythm & Blues Festival, which took place on July 25-27, Ben & Jerry's Folk Festival on Aug. 8-10 and the JVC Jazz Festival on Aug. 16-18. Newport, which helped lift jazz out of smoky nightclubs into the playground of the rich, still holds a special fondness for Wein, whose New York-based Festival Productions Inc. produces about 1,000 music events a year.
FIRST OUTDOOR POP MUSIC FESTIVAL IN AMERICA

"What makes it different is, first of all, it was the first outdoor festival of any kind of pop music in America," he said. "We never dreamed it would take over the whole world, so to speak. Now there must be thousands of jazz festivals."
Back when it all began, "Newport was the Woodstock of its day," Wein said. "There was nothing else (in the 1950s)."

Wein, who formerly ran the fabled Boston jazz club, Storyville, follows three rules for staging a festival: "One, artists that sell tickets. Two, music I love. And three, music that gives me credibility with the critics."

However, he said he finds himself caring less and less about the critics' opinions as he grows older. At Newport, he often tries to mix artists who have never appeared on the same bill together but who all drink from the same musical well. For instance, this year's Rhythm & Blues Festival featured big names like Aretha Franklin and Patti LaBelle alongside relative newcomers like Joan Osborne and veteran blues musicians Cootie Stark and Van "Piano Man" Walls.

"You're mixing up areas of the same music, but the areas are so different that it becomes a unique experience," Wein said. Before the first Newport festival in 1954, he said, the be-bop and swing schools of jazz had never been on the same stage together.
As a man who has spent a lifetime doing the musical equivalent of mingling with the gods on Mount Olympus, Wein's conversation draws from a bottomless supply of anecdotes.

A story about Miles Davis' 1955 Newport performance of "'Round Midnight" somehow glides into a recollection of riding in a car with Mick Jagger and industry mogul Ahmet Ertegun -- which then reminds him of the time he put violinist Stephane Grappelli on the same concert bill with Sly and the Family Stone.
DYLAN GOES ELECTRIC

Asked if he recalled the Newport Folk Festival's most historic moment, he asked incredulously: "Do I remember the day Dylan went electric? I was the one who stood backstage, handed him an acoustic guitar and said, 'You've got to go back, Bob, or there'll be a riot out there.' So he went back and sang two or three songs."

To his immense frustration, Wein has never been able to lure Dylan back to Newport since that historic day. He brought up the idea the last time he saw him, in New Orleans, but the great man was noncommital.
Wein is also agitated over the elusive Tracy Chapman -- an artist he much admires, but who apparently shies away from the festival because she doesn't want to be labeled as "folk."

Another occupational hazard is artists who use the Newport stage as a career launching pad and then defect to competing festivals or travelling tours. The Indigo Girls have foregone Newport this year, as have Ani DiFranco and Mary Chapin Carpenter. "It's difficult, because when they become too popular, they look in other areas," Wein said.

But he takes satisfaction that James Taylor is returning to Newport this summer for the first time in 27 years. And Joan Baez, who rose to fame in the 1959 Newport Folk Festival, is returning on an Aug. 9 programme with younger artists including Mary Black and Dar Williams.

Wein said he knows his own limitations and decided long ago that he did not want to be a rock promoter. "I have too much love and respect for my own festivals. I don't want a crowd of artists taking over who are bigger than the festival."
In 1969, Jimi Hendrix called and begged to be on the bill at Newport, Wein said. "I said, 'I've got no room, Jimi.'"

Ditto Mick Jagger, who once floated a Newport balloon. "I said, 'If you want to come up alone, sing a few songs at the folk festival and not use the Rolling Stones' name, OK. But I don't want the Rolling Stones.'"
